Joint Exploratory Analysis — Continuous and Discrete Numerical Features

This analysis evaluates continuous and discrete quantitative features together because covariance, Pearson correlation and Spearman correlation can be applied to both numerical types.

The distinction between continuous and discrete features is retained for interpretation and visualization.

Total dataset observations: 1852394
Complete finite observations analyzed: 1852394
Observations excluded because of missing or non-finite values: 0
Excluded percentage: 0.000000%

1. Numerical feature overview

FEATURE NUMERICAL_TYPE INTERPRETATION
SEND_AGE Continuous Sender age measured on a numerical scale
TRANS_VALUE Continuous Transaction monetary value
TRANS_DAY Discrete Day of month with values from 1 to 31
SEND_POP_REGISTER Discrete Registered population count
Continuous and discrete numerical variables are analyzed in the same numerical framework. Their classification is retained because the support of a variable affects interpretation and the most appropriate visualization. For example, TRANS_DAY has only a limited set of integer values, while TRANS_VALUE can vary across a substantially finer scale.

3. Covariance matrix

Covariance evaluates whether pairs of numerical variables tend to vary in the same or opposite direction. Its magnitude depends on the units of the variables and should therefore not be interpreted as a standardized measure of association strength.

4. Pearson correlation

Pearson correlation evaluates linear association between every pair of numerical features. The matrix includes continuous-continuous, discrete-discrete and continuous-discrete relationships.

SEND_AGE TRANS_VALUE TRANS_DAY SEND_POP_REGISTER

TRANS_DAY -0.000564 0.000069 1.000000 0.000654
SEND_POP_REGISTER -0.092144 0.004921 0.000654 1.000000

Strongest absolute Pearson relationship: SEND_AGE × SEND_POP_REGISTER = -0.092144.

5. Spearman correlation

Spearman correlation evaluates monotonic association using ranks. This measure is especially useful as a complement to Pearson when relationships are not strictly linear or when extreme observations affect the linear coefficient.

Discrete variables can contain many tied values. These ties are handled through average ranks during the Spearman calculation.

SEND_AGE TRANS_VALUE TRANS_DAY SEND_POP_REGISTER
SEND_AGE 1.000000 -0.024141 -0.000698 -0.155335
TRANS_VALUE -0.024141 1.000000 -0.000334 -0.023803
TRANS_DAY -0.000698 -0.000334 1.000000 0.000132
SEND_POP_REGISTER -0.155335 -0.023803 0.000132 1.000000

Strongest absolute Spearman relationship: SEND_AGE × SEND_POP_REGISTER = -0.155335.

A substantial difference between Pearson and Spearman may indicate non-linearity, asymmetry, rank effects, tied values or sensitivity to extreme observations.

9. Potential redundancy

A numerical pair is flagged as potentially redundant when at least one absolute Pearson or Spearman coefficient is greater than or equal to: 0.90.

FEATURE_1 FEATURE_2 PEARSON SPEARMAN POTENTIAL_REDUNDANCY
SEND_AGE TRANS_VALUE -0.010660 -0.024141 No
SEND_AGE TRANS_DAY -0.000564 -0.000698 No
SEND_AGE SEND_POP_REGISTER -0.092144 -0.155335 No
TRANS_VALUE TRANS_DAY 0.000069 -0.000334 No
TRANS_VALUE SEND_POP_REGISTER 0.004921 -0.023803 No
TRANS_DAY SEND_POP_REGISTER 0.000654 0.000132 No
No numerical feature pair reached an absolute Pearson or Spearman correlation equal to or greater than 0.90. No strong evidence of numerical redundancy is identified at the selected threshold.

Correlation alone is not used to remove a feature during this exploratory stage. Any decision involving feature removal, transformation or dimensionality reduction should be revisited together with the later multicollinearity, PCA and modeling analyses.

10. Summary of results

Numerical features analyzed: 4.

Unique pairwise relationships analyzed: 6.

Strongest absolute Pearson relationship: SEND_AGE × SEND_POP_REGISTER = -0.092144.

Strongest absolute Spearman relationship: SEND_AGE × SEND_POP_REGISTER = -0.155335.

Potentially redundant pairs: 0.

Exploratory conclusion:

Continuous and discrete quantitative variables were analyzed together because the selected covariance and correlation methods are applicable to both numerical types.

The Pearson matrix describes linear relationships, while the Spearman matrix evaluates monotonic relationships through ranks.

Comparison between the two coefficients helps identify relationships that may be affected by non-linearity, extreme observations or tied values.

Visualizations are adapted to the numerical support of each feature pair rather than forcing the same graph on variables with substantially different structures.

No numerical feature is removed or transformed during this exploratory stage.
